title: On Differentially Private Mechanisms for Linear Regression
topic: Social Aspects->Privacy-preserving Statistics and Machine Learning
claim: Our mechanism's loss stays far below competing private baselines over time and approaches the non-private optimum, while the baselines collapse to a trivial solution.
layout: 1 panel, log-scale line plot, time on x-axis, legend top-left
description: A single wide line plot titled 'year_eps2.0'. The x-axis is Time, running from 0 to about 500,000. The y-axis is loss F on a log scale from 10^0 to above 10^6. A legend at top-left lists AdaSSP1/16, AdaSSP1, Batch, PQFTL, non-private and trivial. All curves rise steeply at first and then flatten. The green non-private curve is lowest, at about 10^4 at the end. The dark blue AdaSSP1/16 curve sits just above it, at about 2x10^4. The light blue AdaSSP1 curve is higher, at about 10^5. Batch (magenta), PQFTL (orange) and trivial (black) overlap near 1.5x10^5. The magenta Batch curve has a shaded band and tall spikes up to 10^6. The eye goes first to the gap between the blue curves and the cluster of overlapping curves above them.
caption: Results of the experiment for different algorithms for the year dataset with $\eps=2$. The $y$-axis is the loss $F(\cdot)$ (in logarithmic scale) of different algorithms and the $x$-axis is time. Solid lines show the median over 10 random seeds and shaded regions show the 25-75th percentile range. AdaSSP1 (light blue) is our mechanism according to our theoretical guarantees, AdaSSP1/16 (blue) is a heuristic improvement of it, and Non-private (green) is the non-private optimal answer. All remaining algorithms have basically the same high loss function with some spikes for the Batch algorithm (red).
abstract: We study the classic least-squares linear regression problem under differential privacy (DP) in the batch and the continual observation setting. In the latter setting, the mechanism receives a stream of $n$ data points $(x_i,y_i)$ ($x_i\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and $y_i\in\mathbb{R}$) and must output an estimate of the optimal parameters at each time step $i$. Although differentially private linear regression has been extensively studied in the batch setting, the problem remains underexplored for the continual setting, with prior work being restricted to constrained linear regression and update time polynomial in $n$. In this work, we introduce ContinualAdaSSP, the first mechanism for unconstrained linear regression under continual differential privacy. Our mechanism's suboptimality gap is proportional to $\sqrt{d}\operatorname{polylog}(n)$. It requires $O(d^2\log{n})$ space and $O(d^2\log{n}+d^Ï)$ update time, where $d$ is the dimension of the input space. We also study fundamental limits of differentially private linear regression by showing the first lower bounds for the box-constrained least-squares linear regression problem. Our lower bounds are proportional to $\min(n,\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\log^{1.5}d})$ for $(1,O(\frac{1}{n}))$-DP, and $\min(n,\frac{d}Îµ)$ for $Îµ$-DP, and are derived using a reduction from a fingerprinting code problem from [Peter et al., 2024], providing new insights into the inherent hardness of this canonical task. Our experimental evaluation on real-world datasets shows that the accuracy of our continual observation mechanism clearly outperforms any other known differentially private mechanism for this problem such as rerunning the batch algorithm at each time step.
